# Research Plan: Georgia O'Keeffe New Mexico Landscape Oil Paintings (pre-1940) at the Art Institute of Chicago (as of June 2024)

## Objective
Identify all Georgia O'Keeffe works in the Art Institute of Chicago (AIC) collection as of June 2024 that meet ALL criteria:
- Subject: New Mexico landscapes
- Date: Created before 1940
- Medium: Oil on canvas/board

---

## Phase 1: Primary Source — AIC Collection Database

### 1.1 AIC Online Collection Search
- **URL**: https://www.artic.edu/collection
- **Search Strategy**:
  - Artist: "Georgia O'Keeffe"
  - Filter by classification: "Paintings"
  - Filter by date: before 1940 (use date range or manual review)
  - Keyword searches: "New Mexico", "Taos", "Santa Fe", "Abiquiu", "Ghost Ranch", "Pedernal", "Chama River", "Black Place", "White Place"

### 1.2 AIC Collections API (if available)
- Check for public API at https://api.artic.edu/docs/
- Query endpoint: `/artworks` with filters:
  - `artist_title=Georgia O'Keeffe`
  - `classification_title=Paintings`
  - `date_start=0&date_end=1939`
  - Search `subject_titles` for New Mexico-related terms

### 1.3 AIC Provenance/Collection Records
- Access object records for each candidate work
- Verify acquisition date (must be before June 2024)
- Confirm medium explicitly states "oil on canvas" or "oil on board"
- Confirm subject/description references New Mexico landscape

---

## Phase 2: Published AIC Collection Catalogs

### 2.1 Key Catalogs to Consult
- **Art Institute of Chicago: American Paintings** (various volumes)
- **The Art Institute of Chicago: Twentieth-Century Painting and Sculpture** (1996, 2008 editions)
- **Georgia O'Keeffe: A Retrospective** (AIC exhibition catalog, if applicable)
- **AIC Collection Handbook / Highlights Guides** (multiple editions)

### 2.2 Access Methods
- AIC Library / Ryerson & Burnham Libraries (on-site or digitized)
- HathiTrust / Internet Archive for digitized older catalogs
- WorldCat for locating physical copies
- Google Books / AIC publications portal

---

## Phase 3: O'Keeffe-Specific Scholarly Sources (for Cross-Reference)

### 3.1 Catalogue Raisonné
- **Georgia O'Keeffe: Catalogue Raisonné** (online at okeeffecatalogueraisonne.org) — authoritative source for:
  - Complete works list with dates, mediums, subjects
  - Provenance/exhibition history
  - High-resolution images for visual verification

### 3.2 Key O'Keeffe New Mexico Landscape Works (Pre-1940) — Known Candidates
| Work Title | Year | Medium | Notes |
|------------|------|--------|-------|
| The Lawrence Tree | 1929 | Oil on canvas | New Mexico |
| Black Mesa Landscape, New Mexico / Out Back of Marie's | 1930 | Oil on canvas | |
| Red Hills, Lake George, New Mexico | 1927 | Oil on canvas | Actually Lake George, NY — exclude |
| Ranchos Church, Taos | 1929-30 | Oil on canvas | New Mexico |
| Taos Pueblo | 1929-30 | Oil on canvas | New Mexico |
| The Black Cross, New Mexico | 1929 | Oil on canvas | |
| Near Abiquiu, New Mexico | 1930 | Oil on canvas | |
| Black Place I/II | 1936 | Oil on canvas | |
| Grey Hills | 1936 | Oil on canvas | |
| From the White Place | 1940 | Oil on canvas | 1940 — borderline, verify exact date |

### 3.3 O'Keeffe Scholarship
- Barbara Buhler Lynes publications (O'Keeffe Foundation / Museum)
- Sarah Greenough exhibition catalogs (NGA)
- Lisa Mintz Messinger publications
- O'Keeffe Museum publications (Santa Fe)

---

## Phase 4: Cross-Verification Strategy

### 4.1 Three-Way Match Required
For each candidate work, confirm ALL three:
1. **AIC Collection Record**: Object in collection as of June 2024
2. **Catalogue Raisonné**: Listed as O'Keeffe, pre-1940, oil, New Mexico landscape
3. **Provenance**: Acquisition date at AIC before June 2024

### 4.2 Exclusion Criteria
- Works on paper (watercolor, charcoal, pastel) — exclude
- Works dated 1940 or later — exclude
- Non-landscape subjects (flowers, bones, abstractions, cityscapes) — exclude
- New York/Lake George landscapes — exclude
- Works not in AIC collection as of June 2024 — exclude

---

## Phase 5: Edge Cases & Verification

### 5.1 Works on Long-Term Loan to AIC
- Check AIC "Loans" or "Current Exhibitions" pages for June 2024
- Distinguish between accessioned collection vs. loan

### 5.2 Title Variations
- Search multiple title variants (e.g., "Black Place" vs "The Black Place")
- Check for alternate titles in catalogue raisonné

### 5.3 Attribution Changes
- Verify no deaccessioning or re-attribution between catalogue publication and June 2024

---

## Phase 6: Deliverables

### 6.1 Final Report Format
| AIC Accession # | Title | Year | Medium | Dimensions | New Mexico Location | Acquisition Date | Verification Sources |
|-----------------|-------|------|--------|------------|---------------------|------------------|---------------------|
| | | | | | | | |

### 6.2 Evidence Package
- Screenshots of AIC collection pages (with timestamps)
- Catalogue raisonné entry links
- Catalog page citations
- Provenance documentation

---

## Timeline

| Phase | Estimated Time |
|-------|----------------|
| Phase 1: AIC Database Search | 2-3 hours |
| Phase 2: Catalog Review | 2-3 hours |
| Phase 3: Catalogue Raisonné Cross-Ref | 1-2 hours |
| Phase 4: Three-Way Verification | 1-2 hours |
| Phase 5: Edge Case Resolution | 1 hour |
| Phase 6: Report Compilation | 1 hour |
| **Total** | **8-12 hours** |

---

## Tools & Resources

- **Web**: AIC collection site, catalogue raisonné, Google Books, HathiTrust, WorldCat
- **API**: AIC Collections API (if accessible)
- **Library**: Ryerson & Burnham Libraries (AIC) — consider contacting reference desk
- **Documentation**: Screenshots, PDF saves, citation manager (Zotero)

---

## Success Criteria

- Complete list of ALL qualifying works (zero false negatives)
- Zero false positives (every listed work meets ALL 6 criteria)
- Each entry backed by 3 independent verifiable sources
- Report delivered as Markdown with evidence appendix

## About this artwork

“For me, painting the crosses was a way of painting the country,” recalled Georgia O’Keeffe about the series of compositions featuring Catholic crosses that she created upon visiting the Southwest in 1929. In *Black Cross, New Mexico*, she contrasted the handmade cross, magnified in scale and isolated flat against the picture plane, with the distant brilliance of the sunset behind the rolling hills. O’Keeffe’s cross paintings helped cement her association with New Mexico, to which she would return every summer until she moved there permanently in 1949. The Art Institute organized her first major museum retrospective in 1943, and purchased this painting at the time.

 The Black Place 
## Date:

## Artist:

Georgia O’Keeffe (American, 1887–1986)

## About this artwork

_The Black Place_ features an unusually muted palette for Georgia O’Keeffe’s Southwestern paintings: the composition is dominated by shades of white and gray, relieved only by a thin strip of blue sky at the top. “The Black Place” was the name she gave her favorite location to paint, an area of the Bisti/De-Na- Zin Wilderness (also known as the Bisti Badlands) located approximately 150 miles west of Abiquiu, New Mexico. While she painted numerous images of the region’s rounded, gray hills, here she depicted a low, sandy crest that reminded her of her husband, Alfred Stieglitz, as she wrote to him: “When I see the country in its silvery beauty and forbidding blackness in my memory—it is so often almost as if I see you too—your silvery hair and grey clothes and black cape.”

# The White Place in Sun

[IMAGE: Painting of a close-up view of a pale, pinkish stone cliff with a V-shaped dip against a blue sky.]

## Image actions

[IMAGE: Painting of a close-up view of a pale, pinkish stone cliff with a V-shaped dip against a blue sky.]

## Currently Off View

## Date:

1943

## Artist:

Georgia O’Keeffe (American, 1887–1986)

## About this artwork

Georgia O’Keeffe often painted the dramatic geological formation known as the White Place, or Plaza Blanca, which she could see from a window in her home near Abiquiu, New Mexico. Composed of a white stone that stands out starkly against the colors of the surrounding terrain, the White Place was whittled and smoothed by water and wind over centuries into a striking formation resembling columns, cliffs, and towers. Here, O’Keeffe selected a view that emphasizes a deep cleft between two spires. The V-shaped composition accentuates the interplay between the brilliant blue sky, the eerie white color, and the horizontal striations of the rock.

# Red and Pink Rocks and Teeth

[IMAGE: A work made of oil on canvas.]

## Image actions

[IMAGE: A work made of oil on canvas.]

## Currently Off View

## Date:

1938

## Artist:

Georgia O’Keeffe (American, 1887–1986)

## About this artwork

Georgia O’Keeffe was fascinated by the animal bones, weathered and worn, that she found in the desert in New Mexico. In *Red and Pink Rocks and Teeth* she presented a jawbone alongside two stacked rocks that appear both monumental and indeterminate. The smooth, rounded forms of the red and pink rocks appear in enigmatic relation to one another, as the red pebble appears to recede from the picture plane even though it must be perched on top of the pink stone. Their abstracted forms and warm colors contrast sharply with the bleached, angular teeth and hard, cracked appearance of the jawbone and together construct a modern trompe l’oeil that questions the nature of representation and perception.

# Georgia O’Keeffe

![Image 5: Georgia Okeeffe Stieglitz](https://artic-web.imgix.net/a0b8219d-bd2c-41d2-b99d-58a7549f59d8/GeorgiaOKeeffe.jpg?rect=42%2C42%2C1711%2C1831&auto=format&q=1&fit=crop&crop=faces%2Ccenter&w=750&h=803&blur=1200&sat=20)

Also known as Mrs. Alfred Stieglitz, Georgia O’Keefe, Georgia Totto O’Keeffe, Georgia Totto O’Keeffe, 乔治亚·欧姬芙 Date of birth 1887 Date of death 1986

One of the most influential American artists of the 20th century, Georgia O’Keeffe promoted new ideas of abstraction and helped redefine modern art. Best known for her paintings of flowers and plants—enlarged beyond life-size and precisely painted with bold colors—and for her spare and dramatic images inspired by the landscape of the Southwest, O’Keeffe also took inspiration in the aesthetic and architectural styles that she was exposed to during her time as a student at School of the Art Institute of Chicago.

Although she only spent one year at SAIC, leaving to recuperate from typhoid fever, she developed a loyalty to the institution, exhibiting [her first retrospective at the museum in 1943](https://www-2018.artic.edu/exhibitions/7588). After the death of her husband—photographer and art dealer Alfred Stieglitz—O’Keeffe donated his art collection, including his immense holdings of photography to the Art Institute.

While O’Keeffe incorporated elements from various modernist movements into her work, her style was entirely her own. Her ability to connect and infuse natural and abstracted forms with evocative visual and spiritual qualities contributed significantly to the innovations of American modernism.

O’Keeffe also differed from most other American pioneers of modernism in that she was trained entirely in the United States. Apart from her time in Chicago, O’Keeffe lived in Virginia, Texas, and South Carolina before moving permanently to New Mexico, where she worked almost until her death at the age of 98.

Press Release

# Access O’Keeffe, a Groundbreaking Digital Catalogue Raisonné, to Launch in Early 2026

October 2, 2025

### *Project led by the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum will allow global* *audiences to explore every known Georgia O’Keeffe artwork*.

EMBARGOED UNTIL EARLY 2026–October 1, 2025–(Santa Fe, NM)–Georgia  
O’Keeffe’s digital catalogue raisonné, *Access O’Keeffe*, will make its official launch in  
2026, allowing access to every known work by the artist through dynamic tools, interactive browsing, and real-time research updates.

![](https://www.okeeffemuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/20250925_StaffHeadshot_LNeely-6-731x1024.jpg)

Liz Neely, Georgia O’Keeffe Museum Curator of Digital Experience

Supported by the Institute of [Museum and Library Services (IMLS)](https://www.imls.gov/), *Access O’Keeffe* addresses the limitations of a printed catalogue raisonné and creates a new model for what is possible through a reimagined digital platform. *Access O’Keeffe* provides an accessible, dynamic platform to explore the life and art of Georgia O’Keeffe as a user-friendly, searchable website with high-resolution images, visual descriptions, exhibition histories, archival materials, and research data associated with the artist’s two-volume catalogue raisonné, originally written by the Museum’s founding curator and preeminent O’Keeffe scholar Barbara Buhler Lynes in 1999. *Access O’Keeffe* preserves the integrity of the extensive research by Lynes, while incorporating and citing updates from new scholarship, allowing a reader to trace the ideas surrounding a work.

“A catalogue raisonné has long been considered the final word on an artist’s work. With *Access O’Keeffe*, we’re flipping that idea on its head—transforming it into a living dialogue where new voices, discoveries, and perspectives can continuously reshape what we know about Georgia O’Keeffe,” said Liz Neely, Curator of Digital Experience, who spearheaded the project.

The resulting product, built on a linked data platform (using the open Linked Art data standard), offers entirely new ways to explore O’Keeffe’s full body of work. Visitors can browse by color, shape, or medium, explore the context of works created before and after a specific painting, trace historic exhibitions, create lists of favorites, and download images. In addition to the Museum’s own collection, more than 130 partner organizations have contributed up-to-date information on works in their collections, including the National Gallery of Art, the McNay Art Museum, the Art Institute of Chicago, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the National Museum of Modern Art Tokyo. As new scholarship emerges, the digital catalogue raisonné can be updated in real time.

*Access O’Keeffe* has been carefully envisioned by the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum after years of audience research to understand what both scholars and the public seek in a digital tool. The result is a platform that balances usability for broad audiences with the rigor and integrity demanded by researchers. This vision was brought to life through the user interface design of the Museum’s technical partners, [Design for Context](https://www.designforcontext.com/), ensuring the tool is both intuitive and deeply functional.

“Together we’ve been creating ways to illuminate and expand understanding of the connections between this remarkable artist’s works, the places she cherished, the letters she wrote, the people and things in her life, and the research done about her,” said Duane Degler, principal strategist at Design for Context, who has been guiding the development of *Access O’Keeffe* and its predecessor, the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum’s *[Collections Online](https://collections.okeeffemuseum.org/)*, for eight years. “As we continue to add new types of data, the opportunities for exploratory discovery continue to grow, creating ‘aha’ moments for museum visitors and deepening the research potential for scholars.”

![The viewer appears to be looking at the canyon from an unusual angle, perhaps from below. The image could also be the reflection of the cliffs on the surface of the river. Cliffs rise from all sides, and a triangular patch of light sky fills the center of the image.](https://www.okeeffemuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/CR1503-Radical-Abstraction-3-1-scaled-e1670020357120-770x1024.jpg)

Georgia O’Keeffe. On the River I, ca. 1965. Oil on canvas, 30 1/8 x 40 1/16 inches. Georgia O’Keeffe Museum. Gift of The Georgia O’Keeffe Foundation. © Georgia O’Keeffe Museum. [2006.5.392]

One example of the evolving research will be listed under the work[*On the River I*, ca. 1965](https://collections.okeeffemuseum.org/object/1056/). The painting features sandstone hues swirling around a patch of bright pink sky. The piece had been in O’Keeffe’s personal collection until her death and was then gifted to the Museum by the Georgia O’Keeffe Foundation. The original catalogue raisonné listed the piece as a horizontal or landscape orientation. After an examination by the Museum’s Head of Conservation, Dale Kronkright, he discovered evidence of mounting hardware indicating the piece was hung on its shorter side, in a vertical or portrait orientation. The Museum has hung the painting vertically ever since. The changed orientation will be listed in *Access O’Keeffe* with Kronkright’s finding as supporting evidence.

Select media outlets can attend an exclusive Georgia O’Keeffe Museum [members event](https://www.okeeffemuseum.org/events/online-lunch-and-learn-with-liz-neely/) with Liz Neely, as she delves into this project and the contributions from the O’Keeffe’s digital experience and curatorial teams. This virtual event will be on Zoom on Thursday, October 16, from 12:00 PM to 1:00 PM MT. To register for the event, contact Public Relations Manager Renee Lucero at [rlucero@gokm.org](mailto:rlucero@gokm.org) or 505-946-1063.

## —

Located in Santa Fe, New Mexico, where Georgia O’Keeffe lived the final decades of her life, the O’Keeffe has sites and experiences in two historic destinations, Santa Fe and Abiquiú. Reddish-brown hills sweep across the lower portion of the composition. A few green trees poke out from behind the hills, and the blue form of Pedernal rises above. Stretching over the landscape is a clouded daytime sky.

(Alfred Stieglitz, black ink). Not exhibited until 1937–38 New York (An American Place) exhibition. (Source: Lynes, 1999)

Pastel

##### Materials

Pastel on paper mounted to cardboard, pastel board

Pastel on moderately thick, beige, sand-covered paper mounted to grey cardboard, pastel board
